reports.title: Growing Older by the Lake
reports.subtitle: Needs, Options and a New Way Forward

cover.alt: Illustrative concept of an older couple biking an orchard lane in blossom, with Lake Chelan behind them

reports.card: How the valley’s older population is growing, where care is today, what it costs, and how Apple Blossom Commons is planned to help people stay close to home.
reports.metaDescription: How the Lake Chelan Valley’s older population is growing, where senior housing and care are today, and how Apple Blossom Commons is planned to help.
reports.lead: The Lake Chelan Valley is a place people love to grow older in, and more of them do every year. What’s missing is a way to stay here, close to the lake and to family, as needs change. Apple Blossom Commons is planned to fill that gap.

findings.statLabel: of Chelan County residents are 65 or older
findings.title: One in five neighbors is 65 or older.
findings.text: About 16,800 Chelan County residents (21%) are 65 or older today. State projections put that share above one in four by 2035.

findings.statLabel: more residents 65+ by 2050
findings.title: The older population keeps growing.
findings.text: The county’s 65+ population is projected to rise from about 19,300 in 2025 to about 26,300 by 2050, an increase of roughly 7,000 people (36%).

findings.statLabel: more people aged 65–69 because of moves, 2010–2020
findings.title: People choose the valley later in life.
findings.text: From 2010 to 2020, Chelan County gained more people aged 65 to 69 through moves than it lost, while King County saw the opposite.

findings.statLabel: to most senior housing and care
findings.title: Most care is about 40 miles away.
findings.text: Chelan has one assisted living and memory care community and no nursing home. Most of the region’s senior housing and care is in the Wenatchee area, 45 to 60 minutes from the lake.

findings.statLabel: to the nearest Life Plan Community
findings.title: There is no Life Plan Community in North Central Washington.
findings.text: The nearest one is in Spokane, about 165 miles away, so moving between levels of care usually means moving between towns.

findings.statLabel: a month for assisted living in Washington
findings.title: Budgets vary widely, so options should too.
findings.text: Assisted living in Washington costs about $6,975 a month, more than the typical local older household earns. Home equity, a range of home types and prices, and help for staying at home all matter.

findings.title: Apple Blossom Commons is planned to close these gaps.
findings.text: One community near the lake designed for walking, with homes for every stage of life, care a short walk away, and a village, parks and trails close by.

charts.title: The county’s 65+ population is projected to grow by about 7,000 by 2050
charts.subtitle: Chelan County residents 65 and older. 2020 is census-based; later years are projections.
charts.caption: Growth is fastest over the next ten years as the baby boom generation moves into its 70s and 80s. It slows after 2035, but does not stop.

responds.intro: Apple Blossom Commons is planned so that people can stay in the valley through every stage of later life, close to care, close to family and close to the lake. Moving to the next step means a short walk, not a move to another town.

rows.found: No Life Plan Community in North Central Washington
rows.planned: Orchard Grove, planned as a Life Plan Community: cottages and townhomes for active adults, with more support available in the same community if needs change

rows.found: Most care is about 40 miles away
rows.planned: Heritage Grove, planned next door for independent living, assisted living, memory care and nursing care, so more help is a short walk from home

rows.found: Care feels far from home
rows.planned: Both senior neighborhoods are planned beside the hospital campus, with clinics, therapy and rehabilitation planned nearby in the Wellness District

rows.found: Most people want to stay in their homes
rows.planned: Homes designed for aging in place: single-level living, level paths, wider doorways and good lighting

rows.found: Many don’t want to live set apart from everyday life
rows.planned: Senior neighborhoods that are part of a larger community, next to family homes, parks, trails and a small village of cafés and shops

rows.found: Budgets vary widely
rows.planned: Homes at more than one price, in a range of types and sizes

rows.found: Families and care workers are stretched
rows.planned: Technology that takes on routine work so caregivers have more time for people: virtual visits, home sensors that can alert a caregiver, and robots for routine tasks

responds.note: Apple Blossom Commons will grow in phases over many years, and each neighborhood will come when there is real demand for it. Prices, contract options and timing haven’t been decided yet. We’ll share them as plans firm up.

forYou.audience: If you live in the valley now
forYou.text: The need is close to home. Many of the people who will need senior housing and care in the coming decades are already our neighbors, parents and friends. More options in Chelan would mean fewer families driving to Wenatchee to visit a parent, and fewer couples living apart when one needs more care.

forYou.audience: If you’re planning your own future or a parent’s
forYou.text: Today, staying in the valley as your needs change is hard, because most care is 40 miles away and there is no Life Plan Community in the region. It is worth planning early, learning how different types of care are paid for, and looking at how home equity could help.

forYou.audience: If you invest in or provide senior housing and care
forYou.text: The evidence points to a real gap. The older population is growing, local options are few, and there is no Life Plan Community in North Central Washington. As the first community of its kind in the region, it also brings first-mover questions: pricing and how quickly homes fill will be set without a local example, and the care workforce will need early planning.

forYou.audience: If you buy land or build homes
forYou.text: Homes designed for later life (single-level, low-upkeep, close to services) are scarce near the lake. Active adults in their late 60s and 70s are the largest group of older residents, and most will want homes that keep working as they age, near care but not in a care setting.

reports.title: Care Close By
reports.subtitle: Healthcare, Technology and a Connected Community

cover.alt: Illustrative concept of an older couple walking a garden path past a low timber care building

reports.card: The hospital campus next door, the care people travel for today, and how homes, clinics and helpful technology can be planned together.
reports.metaDescription: The hospital campus next door, the care Lake Chelan families travel for today, and how homes, clinics and helpful technology can be planned together.
reports.lead: Chelan is unusually well placed for a community built around care: a hospital campus right next door, specialists choosing to practice here, and regional virtual care already in place. What’s missing is a neighborhood that brings homes, everyday care and helpful technology together.

findings.statLabel: a hospital campus with 24/7 emergency care
findings.title: Chelan has its own hospital campus.
findings.text: A hospital campus with round-the-clock emergency care sits right beside the Apple Blossom Commons site, and a new EMS building on the campus was set for completion in fall 2026.

findings.statLabel: specialties added at the local hospital, 2025–26
findings.title: Specialists are choosing Chelan.
findings.text: Over the past year the local hospital added dermatology, ear-nose-and-throat and orthopedic physicians, launched a cardiology service and grew its primary care and in-hospital physician teams.

findings.statLabel: to the regional medical center and nursing homes
findings.title: Most other care is in Wenatchee.
findings.text: The region’s larger medical center, and every nursing home in the area, is about 40 miles from the lake.

findings.statLabel: regional virtual care platform launched
findings.title: Virtual care already reaches the region.
findings.text: North Central Washington’s largest health system launched a virtual care platform in 2024, so care by video can build on what is already here.

findings.statLabel: plan to install an emergency response system (national)
findings.title: Older adults welcome technology that helps.
findings.text: Nationally, 64% of older adults plan to install a medical emergency response system to help them live safely at home.

findings.statLabel: projected life expectancy gain in Albert Lea, Minnesota
findings.title: Walkable design is health care too.
findings.text: A town-wide healthy-living effort in Albert Lea, Minnesota, built around walking, was projected to add 2.9 years to residents’ life expectancy.

findings.title: Apple Blossom Commons is planned around care close by.
findings.text: Senior neighborhoods beside the hospital campus, clinics and therapy in the Wellness District, and technology that gives caregivers more time for people.

charts.title: Beyond the hospital next door, most care is 40 miles or more away
charts.subtitle: Approximate road miles from the Apple Blossom Commons site.
charts.caption: For older adults, the distance to care shapes everyday life. A follow-up visit that means an 80-mile round trip is easy to put off.
charts.source: Apple Blossom Commons competitive supply research (August 2026). Distances are approximate road miles.
charts.a11ySummary: Distances from the site: hospital campus next door; regional medical center in Wenatchee about 40 miles; nursing homes in the Wenatchee area 40 to 48 miles; nearest Life Plan Community, in Spokane, about 165 miles.

charts.subtitle: Healthcare workers in the Wenatchee area.

data.label: home health and personal care aides

charts.caption: Senior care across the country faces a shortage of caregivers, and the valley is no exception. Apple Blossom Commons plans workforce homes nearby, and technology that takes routine work off caregivers’ plates.

extraSections.heading: Our principles for technology
extraSections.intro: Technology at Apple Blossom Commons is planned to take on routine work, so the people who give care have more time for the people they care for. Every idea is a concept being explored, guided by five principles.

items.title: People first.
items.text: Technology supports the relationship between residents and their doctors, nurses and caregivers. It never replaces it.

items.title: Residents decide.
items.text: How personal information is used is settled with residents before anything is built.

items.title: Build on what’s here.
items.text: Start from the region’s existing hospitals and virtual care before adding anything new.

items.title: Right-sized.
items.text: Match ambition to a small community: a small hospital with a long reach, not a big-city medical district.

items.title: Together.
items.text: Plan places, people and technology at the same time.

responds.intro: Apple Blossom Commons is planned so that care is part of everyday life: a short walk away, connected by video when that is easier, and supported by technology that gives caregivers more time for people.

rows.found: Most care beyond the hospital is 40 miles away
rows.planned: Senior neighborhoods planned beside the hospital campus, so care is a short walk from home

rows.found: Specialists and clinics are growing locally
rows.planned: A Wellness District with space for primary care, dental, eye care, physical therapy and a pharmacy

rows.found: Regional virtual care already exists
rows.planned: Homes and clinic rooms ready for video visits with specialists

rows.found: Older adults want to stay safely at home
rows.planned: Homes designed for aging in place, with optional sensors that can alert a caregiver

rows.found: Caregivers are stretched
rows.planned: Workforce homes planned nearby, and technology that takes on routine tasks

rows.found: Walking is good medicine
rows.planned: Level paths, trails and a small village designed so everyday errands are a pleasant walk

responds.note: Apple Blossom Commons will grow in phases over many years. All plans and technology ideas described here are illustrative concepts and may change.

forYou.audience: If you live in the valley now
forYou.text: More care close to home helps everyone, not only future residents. A Wellness District next to the hospital campus would mean more appointments in Chelan and fewer drives to Wenatchee.

forYou.audience: If you’re planning your own future or a parent’s
forYou.text: Being near a hospital campus, with clinics and therapy a short walk away, can make it easier to stay independent longer, and gives families peace of mind.

forYou.audience: If you invest in or provide healthcare or senior living
forYou.text: Clinics, a pharmacy and specialist offices next to a growing hospital campus serve residents, staff and the wider valley. Technology is planned to extend people, not replace them, which keeps the model practical.

forYou.audience: If you buy land or build homes
forYou.text: Homes near care and services are what older buyers look for. Designing for aging in place from the start is easier and cheaper than adding it later.

reports.title: Learning from Others
reports.subtitle: What Eleven Communities Teach Us About Building for Later Life

cover.alt: Illustrative concept of an older couple having coffee on a cottage patio

reports.card: Six lessons from eleven communities across the country that built for later life, and how Apple Blossom Commons applies them.
reports.metaDescription: Six lessons from eleven small-town communities that built homes and care for later life, and how Apple Blossom Commons applies them near Lake Chelan.
reports.lead: Communities like the one planned at Apple Blossom Commons have succeeded in small towns across the country. The ones that did best started modestly, connected homes to care, chose beautiful settings and grew patiently over decades. There is no Life Plan Community anywhere in North Central Washington, so we studied eleven elsewhere. They are examples, not promises: each grew in its own place and time.

findings.statLabel: residents today at a community that opened in one building in 1961
findings.title: The best communities started small and grew for decades.
findings.text: Rogue Valley Manor opened in a single building in 1961 and now serves about 1,000 residents. Givens Estates opened with 78 apartments in 1979 and served about 750 residents by 2022.

findings.statLabel: waits for most homes at Wake Robin
findings.title: Being first in a region can build lasting demand.
findings.text: Wake Robin, which describes itself as Vermont’s only Life Plan Community, reports waits of 8 to 15 years or more for most of its homes.

findings.statLabel: occupancy at two well-run communities
findings.title: Well-run communities stay full.
findings.text: Wake Robin’s independent living homes were 92–93% occupied from 2021 to 2023. Givens Estates reported about 99% occupancy across all levels of care in 2022.

findings.title: Cottages lead to care only when planned that way.
findings.text: Where cottages sit inside a Life Plan Community, they are a front door to care. Where they stand alone, no care was added even after nearly 20 years.

findings.title: Setting matters.
findings.text: The communities most like Chelan all sit beside a lake, a river or mountains, and their settings help draw residents from beyond the local area.

findings.statLabel: for the land under 53 affordable senior apartments
findings.title: Affordable senior homes thrive as good neighbors.
findings.text: In Durango, Colorado, land was provided for $10 for 53 affordable senior apartments, run as their own property with their own financing.

findings.title: Apple Blossom Commons is planned with these lessons in mind.
findings.text: A first phase sized to real demand, homes connected to care from the start, affordable homes as good neighbors, and growth over decades beside the lake.

charts.title: Life Plan Communities grew over decades; active-adult homes sold faster
charts.subtitle: Year each community opened, and its latest reported size.
charts.caption: Planning each part of a community on its own timeline, and not building ahead of demand, is the thread that runs through every success here.
charts.source: Community disclosure statements, operator websites and developer announcements, as compiled in Apple Blossom Commons comparable-community research (August 2026).
charts.a11ySummary: Timeline. Rogue Valley Manor opened in one building in 1961 and has about 1,000 residents in 2026. Givens Estates opened with 78 apartments in 1979 and had about 750 residents in 2022. Wake Robin opened in 1993 and had about 400 residents in 2023. Del Webb at Lake Oconee opened in 2007 and had sold 775 homes by 2024. Latitude Margaritaville Watersound opened in 2021 and had sold more than 2,000 homes by 2024.

charts.title: Cottages are about a quarter to two-fifths of independent living homes
charts.subtitle: Independent living homes by type.
charts.note: Givens Estates cottages include its houses and duplexes.
charts.caption: What matters most is the connection: at both communities, cottage residents can move to more support on the same campus.
charts.source: Wake Robin year-end snapshot (2023); Givens Estates disclosure statement (2024).
charts.a11ySummary: Wake Robin: 98 cottages (39%) and 152 apartments (61%). Givens Estates: 126 cottages (27%) and 341 apartments (73%).

responds.intro: No single community we studied combines everything planned at Apple Blossom Commons: a Life Plan Community, a neighborhood with every level of care next door, a hospital campus beside them, family homes, and a small village of cafés and shops. That is why we drew lessons from each, rather than copying one.

forYou.audience: If you live in the valley now
forYou.text: Communities like these grew slowly, over decades, and became valued parts of their towns. Apple Blossom Commons is planned the same way: one neighborhood at a time, as real demand appears.

forYou.audience: If you’re planning your own future or a parent’s
forYou.text: Life Plan Communities elsewhere stay nearly full and some have long waitlists, a sign that residents value having every level of care in one place. Joining an interest list early is common.

forYou.audience: If you invest in or provide senior living
forYou.text: The strongest precedents pair a first-mover position with a modest first phase and an experienced operator. Absorption differs sharply by product, so each part of the plan should be planned on its own terms.

forYou.audience: If you buy land or build homes
forYou.text: Active-adult homes near a lake sell steadily, and faster than care-based homes. Homes planned next to a care neighborhood offer something stand-alone subdivisions don’t.

reports.title: The Village Economy
reports.subtitle: Shops, Dining and Gathering Places for Neighbors and Visitors

cover.alt: Illustrative concept of a produce stand in an open market hall

reports.card: Who a small village would serve, what the valley already has, and how shops, dining and gathering places can grow with demand.
reports.metaDescription: Who a small village at Apple Blossom Commons would serve, what the Lake Chelan Valley already has, and how shops and dining can grow with demand.
reports.lead: The Lake Chelan Valley already has a strong economy built on its wineries, orchards and visitors. A small village at Apple Blossom Commons can serve future residents and the whole valley by adding what’s missing, and growing only as fast as demand allows.

findings.statLabel: visitor spending in Chelan County, 2024
findings.title: Visitors already spend generously in the county.
findings.text: Visitors spent about $675.5 million in Chelan County in 2024, supporting about 6,700 jobs and $71 million in state and local taxes.

findings.statLabel: yearly growth in overnight visits
findings.title: Overnight visits keep growing.
findings.text: Overnight visits to Chelan County grew about 5.8% a year over the past five years.

findings.statLabel: a year in everyday spending by future residents
findings.title: Residents bring a steady base.
findings.text: People living at Apple Blossom Commons are projected to spend about $15 million a year on everyday needs, from groceries and dining to health care.

findings.statLabel: nearby households to future residents, in most categories
findings.title: Neighbors carry most of the demand.
findings.text: The roughly 3,000 households within about five miles outspend future residents about five to one in most categories, so the village is planned to serve the whole valley.

findings.title: The village adds what’s missing.
findings.text: Groceries, coffee and wine shops are already well served nearby, so the village keeps those small and focuses on dining, health care, recreation and everyday services.

findings.statLabel: Lake Chelan wineries
findings.title: A home for Lake Chelan wineries.
findings.text: Shared winemaking space and partner tasting rooms are being explored for the valley’s 40-plus wineries, alongside a hall for weddings and community events.

findings.title: Apple Blossom Commons is planned as a village that grows with demand.
findings.text: Everyday services and health care first, then wine, food and gathering places as neighbors and visitors arrive, with no storefronts built ahead of demand.

charts.title: Nearby households outspend future residents about five to one
charts.subtitle: Yearly spending, $ millions. Estimates of spending capacity, not sales.
charts.caption: That is why the village is planned to serve the whole valley, not only the people who live at Apple Blossom Commons. Hundreds of people are also expected to work on or near the site, adding daytime customers for cafés and services.
charts.source: Apple Blossom Commons consumption and spending study (November 2026), base case, using the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Consumer Expenditure Survey 2024 and Census income data.

charts.title: Food, shopping and recreation make up nearly half of visitor spending
charts.subtitle: Visitor spending in Chelan County, 2024, $ millions (total about $675.5 million).
charts.caption: Visitor spending helps keep restaurants, tasting rooms and shops open year-round for the people who live here. The village’s visitor businesses are planned to open only as visits are measured.

extraSections.heading: Built in phases, tied to demand
extraSections.intro: The village would open in stages, each one when the residents, neighbors and visitors to support it are there. Nothing would be built ahead of demand.

items.title: Phase 1.
items.text: Opens with everyday needs that don’t depend on visitors: a pharmacy and primary care, dining, fuel, offices, coworking and childcare.

items.title: Phase 2.
items.text: Follows the hotel and the first neighborhoods: partner tasting rooms, a market hall, an event hall and shared winemaking space, plus more health care and services.

items.title: Phase 3.
items.text: Adds what needs a fuller community or proven visitor numbers, such as a brewery taproom, a pub and outdoor gear.

responds.intro: The village at Apple Blossom Commons includes the Chelan Wine Village and the Wellness District. It is planned to add to downtown Chelan, not compete with it.

forYou.audience: If you live in the valley now
forYou.text: More restaurants, health care and everyday services close to home, without duplicating the grocery stores, coffee shops and wine shops you already rely on downtown.

forYou.audience: If you run a local business or winery
forYou.text: The village is planned with space for local operators: market hall stalls, partner tasting rooms, shared winemaking and small storefronts. Early conversations with local producers will shape it.

forYou.audience: If you’re planning to live here
forYou.text: Coffee, dinner, a doctor’s visit and a walk on the trails, all within a short stroll of home, in a village that grows as the community does.
A program built bottom-up from three customer groups and phased to signed demand. Health care, everyday services and office users anchor early phases; visitor-driven uses follow measured visitation.

planned.title: Who Chooses Chelan
planned.subtitle: Who is moving to the valley, and why
